thesis: A quick-lube retailer whose revisions are turning up ahead of a dated print, bought at a level rather than at the market. Fetched revisions are **improving +6.0** to a 72.7% bullish share — the largest improvement in the small-cap earnings slate screened today — against a surprise record of +12.3%, +18.1% and +12.3% in three of the last four quarters. Price at 35.90 has just reclaimed the fetched 200-day average of 34.45 while sitting above the SMA20 of 33.17 and SMA50 of 31.10, so the intermediate trend turned before the revisions did. The entry is the reclaimed 200-day itself at 34.50, which is 3.9% below the market and is real support rather than a reflex discount — the 32.00 stop then sits 2.02 ATR away on a fetched 1.2382 ATR, below the SMA20, and the 41.00 target is 0.08 under the fetched 41.08 range high, giving 2.60:1 without stretching any of the three numbers past something the instrument has actually traded.
key_risk: The entry and the catalyst are in tension and that is the main hazard: a fill at 34.50 requires a 3.9% pullback, and if it arrives in the days just before the 2026-11-19 print the position is opened straight into a binary — which is why the instruction halves the size in that case rather than carrying full exposure. If no pullback comes, the idea simply does not trade. Valvoline is also a discretionary-spend consumer name, and with the fetched 10-year at 4.88% and rising, a consumer-weakness print would hit the multiple and the comp at once. The 19.9x trailing multiple on 1.80 of ttm EPS is not cheap, so this is a revisions and trend idea, not a value one.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that 19.9x for a car-servicing chain with low-single-digit unit growth is a full price, the last reported quarter actually **missed** by 4.7%, and buying any consumer name before a print in a tape down 2.34% on the month is paying up for risk. That is answered on the specific numbers rather than waved off: the -4.7% miss is the oldest of the four fetched quarters and the three since all beat by double digits, so the direction of the surprise record is the opposite of the objection; and the entry at the 200-day plus the half-size rule means the price paid is a support level and the exposure into the event is half, not full.

thesis: A licensing business with the strongest revision turn in the slate, taken at a level rather than at the market. Fetched revisions are **improving +7.8** to a 77.8% bullish share, the largest single improvement found in any screen today, and the royalty model is why that matters: Dolby earns per-device fees rather than selling hardware, so an upgrade cycle shows up as margin without capex. Trailing EPS of 4.11 from the four fetched actuals puts it on 15.7x, which is undemanding for that revenue quality. The chart agrees with the revisions for once — 64.66 is above the fetched SMA20 of 63.03, SMA50 of 60.90 and SMA200 of 59.36, all three stacked in order, and only 7.56% off the 69.95 range high. The entry at 62.00 sits just under the 20-day average, the 58.70 stop is 2.01 ATR below it on a fetched 1.6457 ATR and below the 200-day, and the 69.50 target is 0.45 under the range high — so the ratio of 2.27:1 comes out of three levels the instrument has actually traded rather than out of a target chosen to clear the floor.
key_risk: The print is on 2026-11-17, two sessions away, so a fill at 62.00 almost certainly means being long into the event — hence the half-size rule, without which this is a binary dressed as a trend trade. The two most recent fetched surprises are also the two *smallest* (+1.2% and +1.8%, against +19.7% and +40.0% in the older quarters), so the beat margin is compressing even as the sell side warms up, which is the specific thing that could make an improving-revisions idea fail. Licensing revenue is lumpy and concentrated in a handful of OEM counterparties, so one renegotiation moves a quarter.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that a 77.8% bullish share means the upgrade is already in the price and the entry is only 4.1% below a market that is 7.6% off its high — buying two days before a print whose beat margin has shrunk from 40% to 1.2% is paying for an expectation that is already consensus. That objection is the reason the structure is what it is rather than something I can refute: the entry is set below the market at the 20-day rather than at it, the size into the event is half, and the stop is a full 2.01 ATR wide so an ordinary disappointing-but-not-broken reaction does not take it out. If the view were that the revision turn is already paid for, the correct action would be to stand aside, and that is exactly what happens if 62.00 never trades.
